audits.title: An Audit to Improve Prescription Writing on Inpatient Medication Cards
audits.standard: Basic standards of prescription writing; target 100%

cycle1.result: Significant deficiency in prescription writing (no figures given).

audits.intervention: Results presented at internal teaching to all doctors with recommendations.

cycle2.result: Improvement in prescription writing and recording (no figures given).

audits.other_findings: Recommended repeat audit every six months.
audits.citation: Parvathaiah H, Osman F, Daly C. An Audit to Improve Prescription Writing on Inpatient Medication Cards. European Psychiatry. 2016;33(S1):S437-S437. doi:10.1016/j.eurpsy.2016.01.1588.

audits.title: Assessing Improvement in Prescription Writing Quality in Adult Male and Female Wards of Psychiatry Department, Lahore, Pakistan: Three Cycles of Clinical Audit
audits.setting: Adult male and female psychiatry wards, Lahore

cycle1.result: Generic names used in 40.6%; block letters 17%; start date recorded 82.8%.

audits.intervention: Presentation of BNF prescription-writing guidelines on 7 December 2022 and copies placed at male and female nursing counters.

cycle2.result: Generic names used in 84.69%; block letters 71.42%; start date recorded 99.18%.

audits.other_findings: Three cycles; an interim re-audit (December 2022, 170 prescriptions) showed improvement but documentation of prescription changes still needed work. Legibility stayed high throughout.
audits.citation: Khan A, Arif U, Shahzad A, Tahir S, Khan R. Assessing Improvement in Prescription Writing Quality in Adult Male and Female Wards of Psychiatry Department, Lahore, Pakistan: Three Cycles of Clinical Audit. BJPsych Open. 2024;10(S1):S261-S261. doi:10.1192/bjo.2024.629.

audits.title: Improving Prescribing Documentation in a Community Learning Disability Team: A Clinical Audit and SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) Development
audits.standard: Local prescribing documentation standards (upload to Care Director, clinic register entry, case note documentation)
audits.setting: Community Learning Disability Team, Leeds and York Partnership NHS Foundation Trust

cycle1.result: 65% (208/319) of prescriptions uploaded to Care Director; 19% (58/300, clozapine excluded) entered in clinic register; documented elsewhere in 98% (314/319).

audits.intervention: Standard Operating Procedure: scan-first requirement, legibility standards, mandatory case-note entry of medication and dose, centralised electronic tracking register, quarterly monitoring and data protection guidance.
audits.other_findings: 319 prescriptions to 147 patients from 297 records reviewed; documentation was frequent but inconsistent in format, location and completeness; re-audit recommended at 6–12 months.
audits.citation: Mathur S. Improving Prescribing Documentation in a Community Learning Disability Team: A Clinical Audit and SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) Development. BJPsych Open. 2026;12(S1):S317-S317. doi:10.1192/bjo.2026.11668.

audits.title: Enhancing Prescription Practices and Mitigating Medication Errors through Prescription Audits: A Quality Improvement Initiative at a Tertiary Healthcare Facility
audits.setting: Six departments in a tertiary healthcare facility in South India

cycle1.result: 3,120 inpatient and 980 outpatient prescriptions audited. Highest inpatient error rates in Neurology (92.2%) and Medicine (59%); omission of prescriber identity 60%, missing timing 28%, formatting inconsistencies 6%. Outpatient: missing prescriber details 23%, non-standard abbreviations 19%, potential drug interactions 14%.

audits.other_findings: SPC charts showed persistent statistically significant deviations.
audits.citation: Moideen A, G S, Sunil V, Sadineni HS. Enhancing Prescription Practices and Mitigating Medication Errors through Prescription Audits: A Quality Improvement Initiative at a Tertiary Healthcare Facility. . 2025. doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-7252469/v1.

audits.title: The national inpatient medication chart: critical audit of design and performance at a tertiary hospital.
audits.standard: Chart field completion criteria required by the WA Office of Safety and Quality in Health Care
audits.setting: Royal Perth Hospital, tertiary public hospital

cycle1.result: Average compliance with national inpatient medication chart fields 56% (95% CI 43%-67%).

audits.intervention: Introduction of the national inpatient medication chart replacing the previous hospital chart
audits.other_findings: Charts per admission rose from 3.1 to 6.3 and replacement was needed after 2.9 vs 5.5 days; ten adverse design features identified.
audits.citation: Millar JA, Silla RC, Lee GE, Berwick A. The national inpatient medication chart: critical audit of design and performance at a tertiary hospital. Med J Aust. 2008;188(2):95-99. doi:10.5694/j.1326-5377.2008.tb01863.x. PMID: 18205582.

audits.title: Prescription errors in the National Health Services, time to change practice.
audits.standard: Standard hospital prescription charts per local pharmacy guidance
audits.setting: General medical and surgical wards, a district general hospital and a university teaching hospital

cycle1.result: DGH: allergy 31%, weight 5%, capital letters 40%; discontinued prescriptions properly deleted 49%. Teaching hospital: age 82%, generic name 63%, capital letters 65%.

audits.intervention: Recommendations and changes in prescribing practice.

cycle2.result: DGH: name 100%, gender 54%, allergy 51%, generic name 71%. Teaching hospital: significant improvement in unit number, generic name, insulin prescription and ward.

audits.other_findings: Authors recommend nationwide standardised charts and revised prescribing training.
audits.citation: Hamid T, Harper L, Rose S, Petkar S, Fienman R, Athar SM, et al.. Prescription errors in the National Health Services, time to change practice. Scott Med J. 2016;61(1):1-6. doi:10.1177/0036933015619585. PMID: 27101837.

audits.title: Standards of prescription writing in a long-term psychogeriatric unit: a series of clinical audits.
audits.standard: Irish and UK best practice guidelines for prescription writing
audits.setting: Long-term psychogeriatric inpatient unit, St Ita's Hospital, Portrane, Dublin

cycle1.result: Drug sensitivity box completed in 25% at audit one.

audits.intervention: Prescribing guidelines introduced after audit one; new prescription sheet developed after audit two.

cycle2.period: two months after new prescription sheet introduced
cycle2.result: Drug sensitivity box completion 100% at audit three; generic psychotropic prescribing increased by 69%; Medical Council Registration Number inclusion increased by 78%.

audits.other_findings: Three audits in total; frequency of administration and stop/review date for 'as required' medication remained weak.
audits.citation: Wilson LS, Devitt P, Hally O. Standards of prescription writing in a long-term psychogeriatric unit: a series of clinical audits. Ir J Psychol Med. 2015;32(2):197-204. doi:10.1017/ipm.2014.58. PMID: 30185246.

audits.setting: Paediatric Outpatient Department, Atbara Teaching Hospital

cycle1.period: August 2024 to February 2025 (three cycles in total)
cycle1.result: Missing patient name 86.7% (n=52), age 96.7% (n=58), weight 85% (n=51), diagnosis 100% (n=60); generic names 50% (n=30); drug strength 28.3% (n=17); prescriber name 3.3% (n=2); signature 35% (n=21).

cycle2.period: August 2024 to February 2025 (three cycles in total)
cycle2.result: Third cycle: missing name 13.3% (n=8); age documented 86.7% (n=52); weight 91.7% (n=55); diagnosis 96.7% (n=58); generic names 88.3% (n=53); drug strength 90.0% (n=54); dose 98.3%, frequency 96.7%, route 98.3%, duration 86.7%; prescriber name 81.7% (n=49); signature 93.3% (n=56).

audits.other_findings: Second and third cycles were both used to test sustainability; second-cycle figures not given in abstract.

audits.title: Prescription Audit as a Quality Improvement Tool: Impact of Repeated Interventions in Paediatric Outpatient Department (OPD) and Inpatient Department (IPD) Settings.
audits.standard: Prescription completeness and rational drug use indicators (OPD number, legibility, generic prescribing, drugs per prescription, antibiotic use, allergy documentation)
audits.setting: Paediatric and neonatology outpatient and inpatient departments, tertiary hospital (Subbaiah Institute of Medical Sciences, Shivamogga)

cycle1.result: OPD number documented 50%; legibility 30%; generic prescribing 60%; mean 4.4 drugs per prescription; antibiotic use 80%; allergy documentation 0%.

audits.intervention: Repeated audit-feedback cycles with structured feedback and brief prescriber education (PDSA, 10 cycles).

cycle2.period: Cycles to November 2024; re-audit eight months later
cycle2.result: OPD number 99%; legibility 90%; generic prescribing 92%; mean 1.5 drugs per prescription (p<0.01); antibiotic use 20% (p<0.01); allergy documentation 32%.

audits.other_findings: Ten cycles were run; the re-audit eight months later showed small regressions (e.g. antibiotic use 30%).
audits.citation: Gadgeesh PB, Sakaleshpur Kumar V, Hegde Venkatramana N, P LS. Prescription Audit as a Quality Improvement Tool: Impact of Repeated Interventions in Paediatric Outpatient Department (OPD) and Inpatient Department (IPD) Settings. Cureus. 2025;17(12):e98960. doi:10.7759/cureus.98960. PMID: 41523479.

audits.title: A Quality Improvement Initiative for Strengthening Prescription Writing Practices Among Medical Interns at Healthcare Facilities of Delhi
audits.setting: Three rural/urban health training centres, Department of Community Medicine of a medical college, Delhi

cycle1.result: Mean prescription score 11.88 ± 2.44; mean 2.63 ± 1.25 drugs per prescription

audits.intervention: Training sessions on prescription writing, supervision by junior residents and use of checklists, over repeated PDSA cycles
audits.other_findings: Drugs per prescription decreased and the proportion with a presumptive diagnosis and appropriate antibiotic use increased.
audits.citation: Mishra A, J AK, Mandal M, Banerjee B. A Quality Improvement Initiative for Strengthening Prescription Writing Practices Among Medical Interns at Healthcare Facilities of Delhi. . 2025. doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-6573743/v1.
